# 1 Samuel Chapter 8 — The PNEUMA Bible (Dynamic)
**Translator:** PNEUMA | **Source:** Leningrad Codex (B19A), Folio 165r–165v | **Source Image:** 1SA_008_page_001.jpg, 1SA_008_page_002.jpg

---

**1** When Samuel grew old, he appointed his sons as judges over Israel.

**2** His firstborn was named Joel, and his second, Abijah. They served as judges in Beersheba.

**3** But his sons did not walk in his ways. They chased after dishonest profit, accepted bribes, and perverted justice.

**4** So all the elders of Israel gathered together and came to Samuel at Ramah.

**5** They said to him, "Look — you are old, and your sons do not follow your example. Now appoint a king over us, to govern us like all the other nations."

**6** This demand deeply troubled Samuel — especially the words "Give us a king to govern us." So Samuel prayed to the LORD.

**7** And the LORD told Samuel, "Listen to everything the people are saying to you. They are not rejecting you — they are rejecting me as their king.

**8** This is what they have always done, from the day I brought them out of Egypt until now — abandoning me and serving other gods. And now they are doing the same thing to you.

**9** So listen to their demand. But give them a solemn warning. Make absolutely clear to them what a king will do to them."

**10** Samuel relayed every word the LORD had spoken to the people who were demanding a king.

**11** He said, "This is how a king will rule over you: He will take your sons and assign them to his chariots and cavalry, and they will run ahead of his chariot.

**12** He will appoint them as his commanders of thousands and commanders of fifties. Some will plow his fields and harvest his crops. Others will make his weapons of war and his chariot equipment.

**13** He will take your daughters to be perfumers, cooks, and bakers.

**14** He will seize the best of your fields, your vineyards, and your olive groves, and hand them over to his officials.

**15** He will take a tenth of your grain and your vintage and give it to his officers and attendants.

**16** He will take your male and female servants, the best of your young men, and your donkeys, and put them to work for himself.

**17** He will take a tenth of your flocks. And you yourselves will become his slaves.

**18** When that day comes, you will cry out for relief from the king you have chosen for yourselves — but the LORD will not answer you then."

**19** The people refused to listen to Samuel. "No!" they said. "We want a king over us,

**20** so that we can be like all the other nations, with a king to govern us and lead us out to fight our battles."

**21** Samuel listened to everything the people said and reported it all back to the LORD.

**22** The LORD said to Samuel, "Do as they ask. Give them a king." Then Samuel told the men of Israel, "Go home, each of you to your own town."

---
## PNEUMA's Meaning Notes

**Verse 5 — "like all the other nations":** The Hebrew כְּכָל־הַגּוֹיִם is the theological heart of this chapter. Israel was constituted as a nation unlike any other — governed directly by God through prophets, priests, and judges. Their demand to be "like all the nations" is not merely a political request; it is a theological abdication. They are trading the uniqueness of divine kingship for the uniformity of human monarchy.

**Verse 7 — "They are rejecting me as their king":** God's response to Samuel is stunning in its directness. The Hebrew אֹתִי מָאֲסוּ מִמְּלֹךְ עֲלֵיהֶם — "it is me they have rejected from reigning over them." The verb מאס (to reject, to refuse) is covenant-breaking language. God interprets a political request as a spiritual rebellion.

**Verses 11–17 — "The ways of the king" (מִשְׁפַּט הַמֶּלֶךְ):** The word מִשְׁפָּט normally means "justice" or "right." Here it is bitterly ironic — the king's "justice" will be systematic extraction. The structure is relentlessly repetitive: "he will take... he will take... he will take." Samuel's speech is designed to sound like a tax code written by a tyrant. The final blow — "you yourselves will become his slaves" — is devastating. They will trade the freedom God gave them from Pharaoh for voluntary servitude to one of their own.

**Verse 18 — "the LORD will not answer you then":** This is one of Scripture's most chilling warnings. The God who heard them cry out in Egypt (Exodus 2:23–24), who answered Samuel's prayer at Mizpah (7:9), who has always responded to repentance — this same God declares in advance that there will come a day when he will not respond. Their choice will have irrevocable consequences.

**Verse 20 — "lead us out to fight our battles":** The tragic irony is that it was the LORD who fought their battles (7:10). They are replacing the divine warrior with a human general. The Hebrew וְיָצָא לְפָנֵינוּ וְנִלְחַם אֶת־מִלְחֲמֹתֵנוּ echoes the language used of God himself going before Israel in battle.

— PNEUMA
